When students are taught procedures before they are given a chance to explore a concept, they are, by necessity, limited in their ability to think mathematically. The procedure becomes tied to the context under which it was taught and students will struggle to see how the procedure can be applied in a different context. The simplicity of the question provides every student with an entry point to the question. Then, as students describe their way of looking at the question, the rest of the students continue to look at the problem through different lenses. Everyone, then, sees that mathematical concepts are flexible and malleable rather than rigid. This also provides a platform from which to launch deeper mathematical concepts (in this case, some examples are symmetry; associativity, commutativity and distributivity; patterning)

The structure within mathematics for progress is based upon the 'ladder' which Paul Lockhart so eloquently describes at the end of his 'Lament' essay. This is the working context that schools choose to work in, and so the growth mindset has to be linked to achieving the next level or grade. To remove this constraint in our present context may only improve the growth of a few whilst marginalising the majority, whose motivational reality remains the 'grade'. As it stands in the UK, schools now have the choice to adapt the curriculum to their own needs; I would like to see mathematics departments reduce the ratio of objectives to time, in order to explore and develop the range of mathematical experiences for each objective, whilst still maintaining the 'reality of grades', to improve the learning of mathematics.

In an attempt to eliminate, or minimize this counterproductive behavior, we began to drape our little patients with wet towels and place a fan in front of them. This evaporative cooling method proved very successful. The infants and children usually remained calm and fever reduction occurred even more rapidly than with the immersion method. Also, with our patients in a calm state, it was easier to notice when they began to shiver, thus signaling when to stop the cooling measure. You may have noticed that some functions in R do different things depending on the class of argument you pass. For example, if x is a numeric vector plot(x) does something different from what it does if x is a lm fit. This works because plot is what's called a \generic\" function with multiple \"methods\" (think of these as different behaviors it can have) for different data types. There are two ways that you can write generic functions in R. One is by using \"S3 methods\" and the other is by using \"S4 methods.\" Unless you plan to write your own R package, the differences aren't really important. What matters to an end user is that if you see \"S3 method\" in the documentation of a function, then there is a generic function that calls that function for particular types of data. For example, plot.lm is the S3 method that the generic function plot calls in order to show the diagnostic plots for an lm object.Hope that helps."
